doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

title: First gig at age five and the Depression
summary: He played and sang at five for a five-dollar bill in 1938; recalls hard times for working people.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: So what was your first gig? Can you remember what would have been your first gig?

I had a little small guitar and it was in Westport, Indiana, and I played and sang “Hand Me Down My Walking Cane.” I was five years old. And they gave me five dollars, which was an awful lot of money then. A five dollar bill for my fifth birthday, it was just right after my birthday. I had that five dollar bill for years.
It almost sounds like that Elvis story. He was at a county fair or something and he won second prize.

Yes, about the same thing. But it was so neat, God, you know, five dollars. I was born in 1933. I’m 64. So that was in 1938 then, around through there. And five dollars, good grief, a down payment on a car almost.
That’s coming out of the depression. It was what mid-30s I guess. Check my history book. But yeah, that would have to be a nice chunk of money.
Yeah. A real nice chunk. And I can remember everybody scuffling. That was a pretty rough time. Most of my people were into farming so we had plenty of food on the table © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
of sorts, but some of the people I can remember, that was a rough time, for the working man.
